preheader: Niels Bohr tells a colleague off for being logical instead of thinking; Apple Music's 404 page is a working click-wheel iPod with Breakout hidden in Settings; around a dozen banking apps now specifically permit GrapheneOS; investor-owned American utilities charged 22.7% more per kWh than public ones in 2025; Block has a conversational model that has never read a word, only listened; markets were shut all weekend, and the week to Friday took 2.36% off the Nifty and 7.3% off the smallcaps; India's reserves have fallen six weeks running and sit $64.7bn below September's record; Canada's Bill C-22 would let a minister order a backdoor so long as it is not systemically insecure; Malta's 2,628 'prehistoric' cart ruts turn out to be Classical; Google mapped six kinds of forest at ten metres; sampling the tail of the attention distribution recovers 94% of dense accuracy at 50× sparsity; a chicken wing now comes glazed in sour sweets; and a fire hydrant's bonnet colour is a flow rate in gallons per minute.

quote.text: No, no, you're not thinking; you're just being logical.
quote.author: Niels Bohr
quote.note: Bohr said it to a colleague, and the sting is that the two words are normally treated as synonyms. Logic only moves correctly between propositions you already hold; it cannot tell you that one of them is the wrong shape. Most confident wrong answers — human and otherwise — are not logical failures at all. They are impeccable derivations from a premise nobody stopped to look at.

items.text: If anything in your CI pipeline calls `claude ultrareview`, go and look at it today: since 2.1.309 the command requires workspace trust, which means it asks on a terminal and simply refuses anywhere else. Scripts pass `--trust-workspace`, which takes no value and goes *after* the PR number or base branch, or you set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRAREVIEW_TRUST_CHECK=1`.

hn.title: Apple Music 404 Not Found
bullets: The submission is a deliberately broken URL, and that is the joke: ask Apple Music for a page that does not exist and you get a working click-wheel iPod instead of an error. The same thing lives at a real address, `music.apple.com/us/ipod`, and that page's title says what it is for — "iPod 25th Anniversary". The original iPod was announced on 23 October 2001, which is the day this went up.

It is not a picture of an iPod. The wheel scrolls, the playlist plays, and the catalogue is regional: commenters pulled the underlying data and found the US version carrying 1,029 songs by 682 artists. Previews run 1:30 rather than the usual 30 seconds, which iggldiggl notes the iTunes Store has done for longer tracks for years.

Two of the hardware's quirks were reimplemented. Hold the menu key for a second and the "backlight" comes on (russellbeattie). Go to Settings > About and hold the centre button for five seconds and you get the brick-breaker — "a Breakout clone", says oniony, which replygirl points out "was called brick on the ipod". The real 2001 iPod hid the same game in the same way.

The friction is on iOS, where Safari tries to hand the link to the Music app; the workaround in the thread is a long-press and "open". isolay reports an empty screen without a subscription. 911 points for a 404 page, and the comments are mostly people saying they miss the wheel.

hn.title: Around a dozen banking apps began specifically permitting GrapheneOS
bullets: The claim is narrow and worth reading precisely: around a dozen banking apps now *specifically permit* GrapheneOS. Not that the blocking stopped in general — that a handful of banks went and added an exception for one hardened Android build.

The mechanism is the interesting part, and the GrapheneOS account in the thread is blunt about it: most banks never decided to ban anything. "Play Integrity device or strong integrity levels are an easy way to do it", so that is what they used, and the account's reading is that they are "doing the least possible work to implement weak anti-tampering measures". "Nearly all these apps aren't banning GrapheneOS on purpose." An allowlist entry is the fix for a check nobody meant to apply.

What actually happens to users, from the thread, is a four-way split rather than a binary: apps that do not run at all, apps that partly run, apps that run only in the main profile — which a UK commenter says is where most banks land — and apps with full support. One reports a credit-card app that works but loses virtual cards and "remember me". HSBC's app reportedly refuses third-party keyboards outright, leaving Gboard or Samsung's.

Context from the same account: GrapheneOS has been based on Android 17 since June 2026, with Android 17 QPR2 expected in December. The thread's practical conclusion from the UK is that it is easier to change bank than to change phone.

hn.title: Investor-owned utilities charge 23% more for electricity than public providers
bullets: The headline rounds; the table says 22.7%. In 2025 American homes paid 17.8¢ per kWh to investor-owned utilities, 14.5¢ to public ones and 14.1¢ to co-ops. Monthly bills invert that ordering — $146, $130 and $159 — because co-op customers use the most power. Everything comes off the EIA's annual Form 861 survey, 2015–2025, with CPI from the BLS.

The gap is recent. Since 2020, investor-owned prices are up 34%, public and co-op up 19%, inflation up 24% — so in real terms investor-owned prices rose 7.9% while the others fell 4.3%. Almost all of it opened between 2020 and 2023 (25% against 11%); since then the two have risen at much the same rate.

The obvious objection is geography: public power clusters in cities and next to federal dams. Stripping that out narrows the gap without closing it — 22.7% nationally, 19.8% once you drop the hydro states, 17.3% comparing public and co-ops within the same state. California is the extreme: investor-owned prices up 62% to 33.9¢ against nonprofit's 28% to 22.7¢. It does not hold everywhere — nonprofit prices rose as fast or faster in 10 states, and in Alaska nonprofits are simply dearer, 26.5¢ against 17.8¢.

Two numbers the thread kept returning to. Among the 99 utilities serving 250,000 homes or more, New York State Electric & Gas went from 11.5¢ to 22.6¢, up 97%, and San Diego Gas & Electric rose 79%. And reliability runs the same way: 120 minutes without power per home in 2025 for investor-owned, 80 for public, 166 for co-ops, major storms excluded. The page is careful to say it shows what homes paid and not why, while noting that investor-owned utilities earn a return on what they build and the others have no shareholders.

hn.title: Your Phone Is About to Stop Being Yours: 70 Days Until Lockdown
bullets: This is an advocacy site, and worth reading as one. Its case: a Google policy announced in August 2025 will require every Android developer to register centrally with Google before their software can be installed on any certified device — all apps, not only Play Store ones, worldwide, with no opt-out. The countdown at the top of the page read 69 days when fetched; the page itself dates the requirement to 2027 without naming a day.

The registration terms are the substance of the complaint. The site says signing up means a fee, Google's terms, government-issued ID, evidence of your private signing key, and a list of your current and future application identifiers. For an independent developer the last item is the odd one — declaring in advance what you intend to call things you have not written.

For users, the escape hatch is described as deliberately narrow: enable Developer Mode, wait 24 hours, pass several warning screens, then choose a 7-day or indefinite allowance. The site's sharpest technical point is that this flow lives in Google Play Services rather than the OS, so its terms can be tightened without an Android update.

The asks are concrete and tell you who the page is for. Users: install F-Droid, contact regulators, sign the petition and the open letter, fill in Google's own developer-verification survey. Developers: do not enrol, talk others out of enrolling, ship the site's FreeDroidWarn library and countdown banner. Google employees: a tips address, with instructions to use a non-work machine and a non-Gmail account.

hn.title: Dessa: Conversation Model trained only on speech
bullets: Every voice assistant you have used is a sandwich: speech in, text in the middle, speech out. The text layer is where tone, timing and emphasis are discarded, because text cannot carry them. Block's small AI lab removed the layer. Dessa is trained, in its words, “from scratch on nothing but human conversation” — no text corpus and no pretrained model underneath.

It is also full-duplex, which is a design decision rather than a feature list item. It listens and talks at the same time, the way two people on a phone do, instead of taking turns around a voice-activity detector. That is what makes backchannelling possible — the “yeah” you say while the other person is still going — along with laughter and sarcasm, which live in prosody rather than vocabulary.

The efficiency claims are the part that cuts against the scaling story. Block says Dessa picked up language from hundreds of times fewer words than an LLM sees, and that the whole thing was trained on a single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. Inference runs faster than real time, locally, on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better.

What is absent is as informative as what is claimed. No benchmarks, no latency figures, no architecture, no weights. It is not publicly released: there is a waitlist, and early access has gone first to a small group of AI safety researchers — an unusual order of operations for a launch page, and the only signal on it about what Block thinks the risks are.

stories.headline: A quiet week on the benchmarks and a rout underneath: the Nifty lost 2.36% and the smallcaps 7.3%, while domestic funds bought four times what foreigners sold
stories.source: Liquide's weekly review for 19–23 October for the index levels, weekly changes, breadth of the sell-off and the daily FII/DII cash table; Pound Sterling Live's USD/INR history for the rupee; PTI (via The Pioneer) for the RBI's weekly reserves release
bullets: Indian markets were closed on Saturday and are closed today, so these are Friday 23 October's closes and the week that ended with them. The benchmarks look dull: Sensex 73,123.83, down 1,605.44 points or 2.15% on the week; Nifty 22,600.00, down 546.15 or 2.36%. The ranking underneath is what the week was actually about — Bank Nifty −2.79%, midcaps about −5.6%, smallcaps about −7.3%. Fifteen of sixteen major sectors fell.

The flow data says who was selling, and it was not foreigners. FIIs took out a net ₹2,697.37 crore across the five sessions — heavy on Thursday at ₹3,458.70 crore, but buyers again on Friday to the tune of ₹887.65 crore. Domestic institutions put in ₹10,942.19 crore, four times the foreign outflow. A market can fall 2.4% on the week with ten thousand crore of domestic money arriving, and this one did.

The rupee's week is a round trip rather than a slide. USD/INR closed Friday at 94.9500 against 94.6993 on Thursday, a 25-paise fall for the rupee — but Monday's close was 94.9324, so five sessions moved it less than two paise net. The 2026 range on the same series runs from 89.6546 on 7 January to 97.1088 on 19 May.

The number with the longest reach came out on Friday too. India's foreign exchange reserves fell $5.011 billion to $721.016 billion in the week to 16 October — a sixth consecutive weekly decline, with foreign currency assets down $5.758 billion to $591.847 billion while gold rose $706 million to $105.8 billion. That leaves reserves $64.69 billion below the record $785.706 billion of the week to 4 September, the peak that the concessional FCNR(B) swap window built.

trends.headline: India's reserves have now fallen six weeks running, and $64.7 billion of September's record has gone
trends.subject: India's forex reserves at $721.016 bn, down $5.011 bn in the week to 16 October, a sixth straight fall from the 4 September peak of $785.706 bn.
trends.subtitle: PTI via The Pioneer, 24 October 2026, on the Reserve Bank's weekly release of Friday 23 October
bullets: The level is $721.016 billion, down $5.011 billion in the week to 16 October. The week before that it fell $8.578 billion, from $734.6 to $726.027 billion. Six weeks of falls in a row is the part that matters more than any single print.

The composition tells you which way to read it. Foreign currency assets — the big component, and the one the RBI actually spends — fell $5.758 billion to $591.847 billion. Gold went the other way, up $706 million to $105.8 billion. SDRs rose $30 million to $18.578 billion and the IMF reserve position $11 million to $4.791 billion. The decline is entirely in the currency leg.

Six weeks ago these reserves were at an all-time high of $785.706 billion, in the week ended 4 September. The peak was not organic: it was built by a special concessional swap window for diaspora FCNR(B) deposits, and what is draining now is partly the same money going back out. On top of that, analysts quoted in the report attribute the fall to the RBI selling dollars to hold the rupee — which closed Friday at 94.95.

The caveat worth keeping is that a weekly move of this size is not necessarily intervention at all. Reserves are held in several currencies and reported in dollars, so a stronger dollar shrinks the number without a single trade; one market commentary quoted puts moves of this magnitude well inside what valuation effects alone explain. The Pioneer's own framing splits the difference, citing both FCNR(B) outflows and dollar sales.

trends.headline: Canada's surveillance bill has cleared the Commons, and it lets a minister order a backdoor so long as it is not “systemically” insecure
trends.subject: Canada's Bill C-22, the Lawful Access Act, has passed the Commons and sits with the Senate: ministerial backdoor orders plus metadata retention for up to a year.
trends.subtitle: Joe Mullin, EFF Deeplinks, 22 October 2026, drawing on the CCLA and Citizen Lab analysis
bullets: Bill C-22 — the Lawful Access Act — has already passed the House of Commons and is now in front of the Senate, which is the whole reason EFF is writing about it with a clock running. It compels digital services, telecoms and messaging apps alike, to assist government surveillance.

The clause worth reading twice is the backdoor power. Canada's Minister of Public Safety could order a company to build law-enforcement access, with the only stated limit being that it must not create “systemic insecurity”. That is a test that a minister applies to their own order, and it is the argument encryption engineers have spent thirty years saying cannot be satisfied: there is no door that only opens for one party.

Two other mechanisms do quieter work. Metadata retention for up to a year — who you contacted, where you were, which services you used — applies to people nobody suspects of anything; metadata is the part that is cheap to store and most legible at scale. And a negotiated cross-border agreement could route Canadians' data to foreign police, including in the US, without a Canadian court in the path.

EFF is not the technical source here and says so: the detailed constitutional and cybersecurity analysis is by researchers at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and Citizen Lab, who want Part 2 — the surveillance and retention regime in full — withdrawn rather than amended. The ask is a CCLA petition aimed at the Senate. No committee date is given, which is itself the point of the headline.

trends.headline: Malta's stone 'railways' have been read as prehistoric for two centuries. Someone counted all 2,628 of them and found no evidence for it.
trends.subject: Malta's 2,628 cart ruts redated to the Classical era rather than the Neolithic, by Joel Grima across 228 sites on Malta and Gozo.
trends.subtitle: Ancient Origins, 21 October 2026, on Grima in Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, doi 10.1016/j.jasrep.2026.106134
bullets: The ruts are one of Malta's famous puzzles: parallel grooves worn into bare limestone, running across the islands and, in places, straight off the edge into the sea. Weathered rock plus routes that drown equals great antiquity — that has been the reasoning since the nineteenth century, and it put them in the Neolithic or Bronze Age. Grima catalogued 2,628 tracks across 228 sites, about 49.65 km of grooves in total, made 3D models of 155 of them, and found no secure evidence that any single pair is prehistoric.

The decisive evidence is stratigraphic and local. At the Domus Romana in Mdina, tracks run through an urban street that was later buried under successive Roman road surfaces — so the grooves are older than those surfaces and no older. At il-Qortin in Marsa, an eighteenth-century drawing records grooves worn into the threshold slabs of a Roman warehouse. Add 112 cases of quarries cutting across ruts and 17 of traffic wearing grooves into quarry floors, and the sequence puts the carts in the Classical era.

Two of the supporting arguments for antiquity dissolve on inspection. Of 1,690 mapped burials, 34% lie within 50 metres of a known track — which reads as prehistoric association until you notice that roads and cemeteries go together in every period. And the routes that run into the sea: sea level is up about 1.3 metres in 2,000 years and coastal rock has collapsed, which is enough.

It is a negative result stated carefully, which is why it is interesting. Grima does not claim every groove is Roman and does not rule out an older date; he reports that nobody has produced solid evidence for one. Forty-eight of the 2,628 turned out to be modern. A two-century-old date that rested on how old the stone looked has been replaced by a question about which centuries of traffic made which grooves.

research.title: A tree-cover map cannot tell a rainforest from a palm plantation. Google has mapped six kinds of forest at ten metres, and got it right 90% of the time.
research.subject: Google's ForTy map sorts the world's land into six FAO forest types at 10 metres, 90% right on type and 95% on forest versus not.
research.subtitle: Google DeepMind blog, 22 October 2026, with WRI and IIASA; map and time series open on Google Earth Engine
bullets: The problem is a category error baked into every global forest map so far. They measure tree cover, and tree cover cannot distinguish a primary forest from an oil-palm plantation — both are trees. So when a natural forest is logged and replanted, the map registers a dip and then a recovery, and the thing that was actually lost never appears in the data at all.

ForTy classifies rather than counts. Six categories taken from UN FAO definitions — primary forest, naturally regenerating forest, planted forest, plantation forest, tree crops and agroforestry, and other land — at 10-by-10-metre patches, globally. Training used about 1.7 million labelled locations from expert surveys, national and regional datasets, and targeted re-review of places the model got wrong. The key input is AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings rather than raw imagery.

Validation is against more than 9,000 randomly chosen sites: 90% correct on forest type, 95% on the easier forest-versus-not question, which Google says beats other global forest maps. There is also a time series, one layer per year from 2017 to 2025, which is where the conversions show up — natural forest becoming plantation or farmland, the transition the old maps could not see.

The reason this ships now rather than as a paper is regulatory. The EU's deforestation regulation uses 2020 as its baseline, and ForTy 2020 is built to that year — companies and regulators need to say what was standing on a plot six years ago, by type. Map and time series are free on Google Earth Engine under an open licence, which makes the compliance question auditable by anyone, not just the firms being audited.

research.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
research.subject: Stratified Sparse Attention recovers 94% of dense accuracy on RULER-HARD at 32K with 50× sparsity, and 2.96× faster decode at a million tokens.
research.subtitle: Sahil Joshi, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Aditya Desai and colleagues; arXiv:2610.28441, submitted 20 October 2026; code open-sourced
bullets: The bottleneck in long-context inference is not the model, it is the KV cache: attention has to look at everything stored, and the store keeps growing. Sparse attention is the standard answer — only look at some of it — and it comes in two flavours that fail in opposite directions. Deterministic top-k retrieval picks the highest-scoring tokens and simply throws away the attention mass sitting in the tail. Sampling covers the tail but adds variance. Hybrids of the two still fall well short of dense attention once you push sparsity hard.

The move is to stop choosing. Stratified Sparse Attention attends deterministically to the top scorers, then *samples* the rest using cheap proxy scores and corrects each sampled token by its own inclusion probability — an importance-weighting trick that makes the sample an unbiased estimate of the mass it stands for. Top-k, top-p and the top-k-plus-uniform hybrids all fall out as special cases, which is the cleanest kind of result: the existing methods were corners of a space nobody had written down.

The numbers are where it earns the paper. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B at 50× attention sparsity, 32K context: 84.2% against the strongest practical baseline's 81.8%, which is 94% of dense performance. The harder case is more telling — at 128K, 69.3% against 63.8%, recovering 85% of dense. The gap to dense widens with context for everyone; this narrows it by about a third of what was left.

It is also engineered rather than just proposed. Custom CUDA kernels give up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at a million tokens of context, tested across five models from 3B to 27B on RULER, LongBench, LOFT and AIME, with the code open-sourced. No perplexity figures in the abstract — the claims are task accuracy and wall-clock, which for this problem are the honest ones to make.

wild.headline: Wingstop has glazed chicken wings in sour sweets, and the crew who tried them called it good but weird
wild.subject: Wingstop put a redberry sour-sweet glaze topped with pulverised candy on wings, tenders and boneless, 23 October to 5 November.
wild.subtitle: Dani Zoeller, The Takeout, 21 October 2026, tasting it at a central Florida store
bullets: The product is a deep red glaze — fruity, sweet, tart — with pulverised Sour Patch Kids scattered over the top, offered across boneless wings, bone-in wings and tenders rather than quarantined to one format. Club Wingstop members got it on 23 October, everyone else from 27 October, and it goes on 5 November or when it runs out.

It is not spicy, which is the detail that explains the whole thing. The reviewer's comparison is orange chicken with berry in place of citrus — and once you put it that way, a sweet-sour fruit glaze on fried chicken stops being a Halloween gag and becomes a thing most takeaway menus already sell. The joke is the branding; the flavour is conventional.

Priced like any other flavour: a 10-piece combo came to $15.79 boneless or $17.19 bone-in at one central Florida store. No premium for the stunt, which suggests the candy is a marketing cost rather than an ingredient cost.

The best line in the piece is not from the brand. Wingstop's own crew, who had eaten it, told the reviewer it was good but weird — which is a more useful review than the press release, and her verdict agreed: “Yes, these are ridiculously good.” It also launches the candy brand's “13 Days of Mischief” run-up to Halloween, so two marketing calendars are being settled with one sauce.

wild.headline: Yakiniku Like has built a seat whose whole purpose is filming, and will not charge you to use it
wild.subject: Yakiniku Like opened a filming-and-streaming seat, Studio Like, at its Shinjuku South store, free in 60-minute slots for two.
wild.subtitle: AdverTimes, 21 October 2026; reservations opened 8 October, collaboration set ¥1,870 including tax
bullets: Restaurants spend real effort discouraging this. Yakiniku Like went the other way and built the seat: "Studio Like: Iwata Mari's Room", open since 19 October at its Shinjuku South store, with a bright vanity-style mirror light for faces, an overhead camera rig pointed at the hands cooking the meat, and a backdrop. Live streaming is supported rather than tolerated.

The design was researched rather than guessed. The chain studied how its collaborating talent, Iwata Mari, actually films, and went through social posts from its own customers and from food-review accounts to work out which angles and compositions people were already attempting — then built the fixtures for those shots. The overhead rig exists because the hands-on-the-grill shot is the one everybody tries and nobody gets.

The terms are the most interesting part. No extra fee, no minimum order: 60-minute slots, two people maximum, booked through the store's LINE account up to the day before. There is a ¥1,870 collaboration set — the "Iwata Mari Aaa Ra Hotpot-Style Yakiniku Set" — but you are not obliged to buy it. The chain is giving away a fully-lit studio for an hour in exchange for the footage existing.

The constraint published with it is the one that makes it workable: streams and photographs must not include staff or other customers. That is the whole problem with filming in restaurants, solved by a floor plan rather than a policy. Yakiniku Like runs 72 stores in Japan as of end-August 2026, one smokeless grill per person, and sells itself as yakiniku fast food — a format that already assumes you are eating alone, which is exactly the customer who films.

wild.headline: Miracle Cocktails spent twelve years licensing Christmas to other people's bars. It has finally done Halloween.
wild.subject: Miracle Cocktails licensed The Haunting, a Halloween pop-up, to bars worldwide after twelve Christmas-only years.
wild.subtitle: Miracle Cocktails via PR Newswire, 11 August 2026; flagship opened 1 October, participating bars ran to 31 October
bullets: The business here is stranger than the decorations. Miracle Cocktails does not run bars. It licenses a season: since 2014 it has rented its Christmas concepts — Miracle and Sippin' Santa — to more than 300 bars worldwide, which hang the décor, pour the prescribed menu and sell the collectible mugs. Miracle is on its twelfth season at over 150 locations. Franchised Christmas, with a cocktail list as the franchise document.

What it has never done is any other holiday, which is what makes this the news. The Haunting is the first expansion beyond Christmas in twelve years, running 1 to 31 October with a flagship at The Cabinet Mezcal Bar in New York. Founder Greg Boehm's framing is explicit about what is being proved: Miracle "is no longer just a Christmas brand. It's a category."

The product that actually moves is glass, not liquid. Sister company Cocktail Kingdom makes the drinkware, sold only at participating locations, and every guest gets a seasonal shot in a collectible shot glass to keep. The cocktails — Widow's Whisper, Scream-sicle, Poison Apple, Liquid Lobotomy, Clown Pear-anoia — are developed centrally by VP Joann Spiegel, so a bar in another country pours the same five drinks from the same spec.

The press release is studiously vague about scale: "cocktail bars across the globe", no count, no cities beyond the flagship, with the list pushed to a website. For a first season that is the sensible disclosure. A twelve-year-old Christmas business testing whether its real asset is the Christmas or the pop-up is a more interesting experiment than the puns suggest.

learn.title: The colour of a fire hydrant is a number. The bonnet tells a firefighter how many gallons a minute they can expect before the hose is off the truck.
learn.subject: A hydrant's bonnet colour encodes rated flow at 20 psi: light blue above 1,500 gpm, green 1,000, orange 500, red under 500.
body: A fire hydrant is painted the way it is to be read at a distance, by someone in a hurry, and the thing being communicated is a flow rate. NFPA 291 asks that the bonnet and the nozzle caps be colour-coded by the hydrant's rated capacity, measured at 20 psi residual pressure: light blue is Class AA, 1,500 gallons a minute or more; green is Class A, 1,000 to 1,499; orange is Class B, 500 to 999; red is Class C, under 500. The standard files Class C under "inadequate", which is a brave thing to write down about a piece of public infrastructure. A crew pulling up to a street corner can read the water supply off the paint.

The barrel carries a different message. The 2019 edition says all barrels are to be chrome yellow "except in cases where another color has already been adopted", and recommends reflective paint so the thing can be found at night. That is why a hydrant painted some other colour on a public street is worth a second look: red usually means private, which the standard asks for deliberately so that crews know whose water they are about to use, and violet — this one is OSHA's recommendation rather than NFPA's — means the water is not drinkable. Texas has legislated black for hydrants that do not work.

The reason the colours are those colours is the least technical and most satisfying part. The scheme was chosen, in the standard's own words, to provide simplicity and consistency "with colors used in signal work for safety, danger, and intermediate condition" — that is, borrowed wholesale from railway signalling, so the meanings were already in people's heads. San Francisco goes further and encodes the source: its Auxiliary Water Supply System, built after the 1906 earthquake, uses blue, black or red caps depending on where the water comes from, and there is a single gold hydrant near Dolores Park painted that way because it kept working when the rest of the city's mains had failed. The honest caveat is that all of this is advisory — local authorities override it constantly — so kerbside hydrant-reading is a convention, not a law.

ideas.prompt: Ten warning labels that should exist
ideas.note: Altucher's drill: ten against one prompt, written fast, not defended. Reddit rate-limited the fetcher after the first subreddit, so the raw material is that week's r/SomebodyMakeThis posts plus four Ask HN idea threads and Y Combinator's Requests for Startups. Reading them, nearly every request was for something that would notice on the reader's behalf — store my own data locally, keep one conversation in one place, remember what I was about to do. A warning label is the cheapest possible version of that: the notice arrives before the mistake instead of after it. Eight are mine; two are marked.

items.text: On every free trial: "Signing up takes one screen. Cancelling takes four."
On a sofa in a showroom: "Measure the stairwell, not the room."
On a second coffee after four o'clock: "This is a loan, not a gift."
On a reply-all button: "Contains 340 people who did not ask."
On a hobby's starter kit: "For most buyers, the kit is the hobby."
On a 6am flight: "Add the taxi to the airport, then compare the fares again."
On a kitchen gadget: "Hand wash only — which is the job you bought this to avoid."
On a houseplant: "Needs light. Will not mention when it stops getting any."
On a note-taking app: "You will move out of here within two years. Nothing here is built for leaving."
items.why: Half of this week's r/SomebodyMakeThis asks were for a better place to keep things; none asked what happens to the last place.

items.text: On an AI chat window: "Everything you type here is stored somewhere you cannot open."
items.why: Adapted from the top r/SomebodyMakeThis post this week, which wanted local data storage for AI and chat apps.
